title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Retreating
dek: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.
why: Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.
who: People concerned with media change, the quality of public discourse and education; product, content and policy practitioners who want to understand the mechanism of how screens change the way we argue.
skip: The section from 53:16 on pop music and reading, whose argument is looser — the conclusion alone is enough.

points.h: Literacy is historically extremely recent and fragile
points.body: Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain ancient Mesopotamian city-state there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read them, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed extreme emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

points.h: The Reading Revolution really did change political form
points.body: Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs, and political affairs were essentially court secrets discussed among a small elite; by the late 18th and early 19th centuries, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

points.h: Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
points.body: Marriott concedes books are imperfect, but argues that the way books organise information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, externalising part of your mind onto the page and then testing it; the reader faces a fixed text and can reread and critically analyse it. More crucially, books restrict the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf was unreadable even to Nazi elites, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; yet Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and regarded as an extremely powerful argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on screen than in a book.

points.h: The Republic of Letters filtered out trolls through writing
points.body: The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote letters to one another and founded journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr rates it enormously highly, even calling it the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if clever people sit alone in a village, their ideas can only be told to their neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into a central pool, and thought grew more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — conversing with Adam Smith, David Hume or Newton sets a high bar, a kind of "submission to something that cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot burst in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will pay attention to you.

points.h: The novel gives us a passage into other minds
points.body: Marriott argues there is a truth about life reachable only through prose fiction: it lets us see the inside of other people's minds. Reading is an active rather than passive process — you build images in your head from the words on the page, which is why it is immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because it gives you the external world and cannot enter another mind directly; and writing is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, mind communicating with mind. He also notes that oral poetry takes little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to "inhabit another mind" appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, holding that great film can get close through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity conveyed by something other than dialogue.

points.h: The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
points.body: Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator, unlike the print-era public intellectual, does not explain and analyse the world but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable stories for an entranced audience. Roberts considers this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable statements online, people habitually interrogate them by the author's standards — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are simply not in that business. Their job is to entertain the audience; truth does not matter, what matters is a story that enthrals. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, driving to a rational conclusion — these are not in fact natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade someone is to entertain him, move him, get angry at him. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

points.h: The richness of pop music also feeds on reading
points.body: Roberts cites an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: the opening of Jagger's "Sympathy for the Devil" is taken directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — the novel opens with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and faith, after which a suave gentleman appears, they take him for mad, and finally realise he is Satan. Marriott calls it an "annoyingly good" example and regrets not having put it in the book. He concedes it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you must move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research showing that over the past 20 years pop songs have grown less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours the simple and the immediate: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

points.h: The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
points.body: Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s, television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the first scroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see whether it lasts — and concedes his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from an analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport, I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.
